verdicts.trueWording: scholarly treatise; conflicting sources make Gyldayn an unreliable narrator
verdicts.note: Claim carries no quote field, so no verbatim string to check; every limb is on the raw article source (fetched via ?action=raw): 'Rather than a novel, Fire & Blood takes the form of a scholarly treatise about the Targaryen dynasty written by a historian within the world of A Song of Ice and Fire, Archmaester Gyldayn' and 'Gyldayn cites a variety of fictional primary sources for the historical events he describes, whose accounts sometimes conflict with each other, reflecting medieval methods of historiography and thus making Gyldayn an unreliable narrator from the reader's perspective.' Graded SUBSTANCE only because there is no supplied quotation to verify word for word.

verdicts.trueWording: a masterpiece of popular historical fiction
verdicts.note: All three attributions verbatim in the Reception section: 'Hugo Rifkind of The Times described it as "interminable, self-indulgent crap."'; 'Dan Jones of The Sunday Times praised the book, calling it "a masterpiece of popular historical fiction"'; 'Chris Lough of Tor.com described the book as "... the best Song of Ice and Fire book in 18 years"'. Verified on Wikipedia itself (the named url), not on the paywalled Times pieces or the dead Tor.com page; Wikipedia's own citation template misspells the Times critic as 'Rifkin, Hugo' while the article body reads Rifkind.

verdicts.trueWording: eldritch epochal terms such as the Doom of Valyria
verdicts.note: Kirkus: 'Martin aficionados are used to eldritch epochal terms such as the Doom of Valyria and the Dance of the Dragons, here evoked as defining points in the emergence of his Targaryen dynasty'. Quote verbatim; both named epochs present. Note the page frames the terms as familiar to aficionados and 'here evoked as defining points' — the claim's 'leans on' is a fair but slightly stronger gloss.

Kirkus: 'Over the span of 700-odd pages...' and 'there are plenty of fierce dragons, impaled bodies, and betrayals to keep the storyline moving along briskly.' Quote verbatim; the 700-page span and all three of dragons/impaled bodies/betrayals confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: even when they don't have any dialogue
verdicts.note: Grimdark: 'George remains perfectly capable of creating vivid personalities that leap from the page even when they don't have any dialogue or appearance on page save descriptions about them.' Quote verbatim; every limb (leap from the page, no dialogue, no on-page appearance, description only) supported.

Grimdark: 'Was Aegon I's eldest child really his or a singer's? Was Maegor the Cruel resurrected as a zombie?'; 'leaves all manner of breadcrumbs as well as clues'; 'the book often offers their own suggestions as to what might have happened.' Quote verbatim; the claim's 'Aegon's heir' renders the page's 'Aegon I's eldest child'.

verdicts.trueWording: A summary of the good parts
verdicts.note: Grimdark: 'George is smart enough to keep all the salacious and twisted details about the Targaryens intact throughout the text while real-life history often downplays these elements'; 'This is not a novel but more a very well-done pseudo-history of events. A summary of the good parts, really, that is done in an entertaining and well-formatted style.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: more like a real work of history
verdicts.note: Speculiction: 'In short, Fire and Blood reads more like a real work of history, whereas The Silmarillion reads more like a collection of interlinked fables/myths—very different.' Quote verbatim; the claim drops the comparative 'more' but keeps the contrast that carries it.

verdicts.trueWording: The narrative is tight, end to end
verdicts.note: Speculiction: 'Fire and Blood reads energetically and dynamically--the Martin of "old". Technique wise, he is on top of his game. The narrative is tight, end to end, and its goals and movement are clear. The same cannot be said of Feast for Crows or Dance with Dragons.' Quote verbatim; all four limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: he is being gossipy about it too
verdicts.note: Jeroen: 'the conceit is that this is a history told by some Maester who is loyal to the crown. The text receives an extra layer of interpretation here where the Maester decides what he wants to tell, or to suggest, and he is being gossipy about it too.' Quote verbatim; every limb (crown-loyal maester, tell-or-suggest, gossipy, extra layer of interpretation) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: as a work by a gossipy historian
verdicts.note: Jeroen: 'makes Fire & Blood tonally completely different from The Silmarillion, because that one is written in a mythopoetic mode. Fire & Blood isn't written as if it is the King James Bible, but as a work by a gossipy historian.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: with just a couple of lines and details
verdicts.note: Jeroen: 'what impresses the most is how Martin is able to sketch out loads of colorful, lively characters with just a couple of lines and details.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: all the names of lords and knights: eyes glazed over
verdicts.note: Quote 'a wash of names' is verbatim, twice: 'It all becomes a wash of names' and 'the impact of battles gets muddled up in a wash of names' — the second limb is fully supported. The first limb is supported in other words: 'with all the names of the lords and knights my eyes glazed over'. The page never says these names come in BATTLE ROSTERS (string 'battle roster' absent); it attributes the glaze to the lords' and knights' names generally and links battles to the name-wash in a separate sentence. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM for that compression.

Jeroen: 'there are many things that Martin doesn't tell you outright but only hints at. For instance, when one queen is rumored to be a witch and over time all her rivals die in mysterious circumstances. It might just slip past if you're not looking out for these hidden plot threads.' Quote verbatim; the parenthetical example and the inattentive-reader limb both supported.

verdicts.trueWording: placed two opposing stories side by side
verdicts.note: Book Analysis: 'Sometimes, Gylndale placed two opposing stories side by side, like that of King Jaehaerys and Alyssane Targaryen.' Quote verbatim. The non-adjudicating limb is supported: 'this leaves the reader to choose between what version of events they want' and 'gives the reader a choice to take what version of an event they want'. Flag: the page misspells the archmaester as 'Gylndale' — the string 'Gyldayn' does not occur on it — but the referent is the book's principal writer, so the claim's canonical spelling is the source's error, not an unsupported limb.
